A Conversation With Sarah Perry

Sarah Perry is a contributing editor at Ribbonfarm , and the author of Every Cradle is a Grave: Rethinking the Ethics of Birth and Suicide (Nine-Banded Books, 2014). Perry occupies a Gertrude Stein-esque role in the intellectual community of post-rationalism, helping bring people together into a salon-like digital space while also producing vitally important work of her own. Perry’s writing has dealt with issues ranging from existentialist ethics and ritual practice to aesthetics, and has appeared (in addition to Ribbonfarm ) in Carcinisation, The View From Hell , and Front Porch Republic. Her writings from 2008-2017 have been anthologized by Not Nothing.

Every Cradle Is a Grave by Sarah Perry

Summary and Review by StoryShots
Having a child means betting someone else's entire life on your own optimism.

Introduction

Being born feels like a gift nobody had to earn.
That assumption collapses under scrutiny: birth is an imposition nobody agreed to, one that arrives with suffering already built into the contract.
That is the thesis of Every Cradle Is a Grave, Rethinking the Ethics of Birth and Suicide, by Sarah Perry, a book that treats birth and death as two sides of the same unresolved ethical problem.

Suicide Is Not Free, No Matter What the Law Says

Most people assume suicide is legal, so anyone who truly wants to die simply can.
That assumption falls apart the moment someone tries.
Involuntary hospitalization, forced medication, and relentless social pressure turn a supposed right into an obstacle course.

Final Summary

This summary of Every Cradle Is a Grave traced the false freedom of suicide law, the manufactured nature of meaning, and the unconsented risk every child inherits at birth into one argument about who really benefits from the stories we tell about life.
